basis: two ways of life and death
note: The commentary prays for the path of the graced and distinguishes it from the astray; the Didache opens by naming two ways, one of life and one of death, giving an early Christian ethical frame for that choice.

basis: Matthean debt as sins before the heavenly King
note: In his homily on Matthew 18:23–35, Chrysostom reads the enormous debt as sins forgiven by the heavenly King and the fellow servant's debt as an interpersonal claim. This interpretation makes the parable's monetary reckoning a moral account.

basis: ransom beyond silver or gold
note: The commentary says a person's offered equivalent cannot settle the final account; Peter says believers were ransomed from futile inherited conduct not with silver or gold, giving a Christian account of redemption whose means differs from a cash equivalent.

basis: Christ's costly blood
note: The commentary says the balance is not tilted by a substitute offered on judgment day; Peter identifies Christ's precious blood as the ransom price, a Christian atonement reading that locates redemption in another's life rather than the debtor's payment.

basis: account before judge of living and dead
note: The commentary's day leaves no one absent from the account; Peter says people will give account to the one ready to judge the living and the dead, tying accountability to the whole human span.

basis: account to the judge of living and dead
note: Those opposed to believers will give an account to the one ready to judge the living and the dead. It provides the commentary's account, universal judge, and resurrection horizon in one formula.

basis: day of the Lord arrives like a thief
note: Paul says the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night. It makes the commentary's day an arriving event that overtakes people rather than an abstract date.

basis: sudden destruction with no escape
note: The claim of peace and safety is followed by sudden destruction that cannot be escaped. This gives the prior day-of-the-Lord image its inescapable consequence.

basis: each receives for deeds before Christ's tribunal
note: The commentary says the day is an individual account with no one absent; Paul says all must appear before Christ's judgment seat to receive for what they did in the body, specifying personal recompense.

basis: all appear to receive what is due
note: All must appear before Christ's judgment seat to receive what is due for deeds done in the body. It combines the commentary's public standing, account, and equivalent return.

basis: leaving the straight way
note: The commentary contrasts a straight path with those who stray; Peter says false teachers have left the straight way and followed Balaam's path, giving apostasy a concrete route image.

basis: day comes; created order passes and works are exposed
note: The day of the Lord arrives like a thief, the heavens and elements pass away, and the earth's works are exposed. It enlarges the commentary's day-as-event into a cosmic disclosure of deeds.

basis: affliction repaid to afflicters
note: The commentary glosses din as recompense and anger as punishment; Paul says God repays affliction to those who afflict, making retribution a balancing of harms.

basis: God repays affliction to afflicters
note: God is said to be just in repaying affliction to those who afflict believers. This is a specific final-judgment use of the commentary's reciprocal payment and punitive wrath.

basis: punishment at the Lord's revelation
note: The commentary interprets divine anger as punitive consequence; Paul describes punishment when the Lord Jesus is revealed, placing that consequence at an eschatological appearance.

basis: appointed day; judge; resurrection
note: The commentary calls the day an event that arrives and links it to rising; Paul says God appointed a day to judge the world through the raised man, joining the fixed day, judgment and resurrection.

basis: God fixed a day to judge the world
note: Paul announces a day fixed for judging the world in righteousness, guaranteed by resurrection. It is a direct day-of-judgment and resurrection formulation alongside Mālik yawm al-dīn.

basis: wrongdoer repaid without partiality
note: The wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong done, with no partiality. This supplies a concise Christian statement of impartial retribution that matches the commentary's exact-scale logic.

basis: Deuteronomy's vengeance applied as warning
note: The commentary glosses divine anger as punishment and dīn as recompense; Hebrews quotes “vengeance is mine, I will repay” and “the Lord will judge his people” from Deuteronomy to warn its hearers, giving those Hebrew formulas a Christian judgment setting.

basis: make straight paths for feet
note: The commentary asks for guidance on a straight path; Hebrews tells its hearers to make straight paths for their feet so the lame may be healed, turning the path image into communal moral practice.

basis: every transgression receives just retribution
note: Hebrews says every transgression and disobedience received a just retribution. It states the commentary's dīn as measured return in juridical rather than commercial language.

basis: no creature hidden; all exposed before God
note: Hebrews says no creature is hidden and all are laid bare before the one to whom account is due. It is a close counterpart to the commentary's insistence that no one can evade the day.

basis: death followed by judgment
note: The commentary makes the day of account universal and unavoidable; Hebrews says people die once and after that comes judgment, adding a concise sequence of death and reckoning.

basis: Christ bears sins; appears to save
note: The commentary says no offered substitute is accepted on the judgment day; Hebrews says Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many and will appear to save those awaiting him, setting out a Christian mediating account while placing the offering before the second appearance.

basis: mercy triumphs over judgment
note: The commentary recalls that a victim's kin may forgive and that payment should be gracious; James says judgment is without mercy to one who showed no mercy, while mercy triumphs over judgment, linking interpersonal mercy to the final account.

basis: withheld wages cry out to the Lord of hosts
note: The unpaid wages of laborers cry out and their cries reach the Lord of hosts. It transfers the commentary's honest trade and unresolved claim into a social injustice heard by divine authority.

basis: Isaiah's straight way applied to John
note: The commentary's prayer is for guidance on a straight path; John identifies the wilderness voice with Isaiah's call to make the Lord's way straight, interpreting the path as preparation for the Lord's arrival through John the Baptist.

basis: those in tombs hear the voice
note: The commentary's standing scene presupposes the dead are raised; Jesus says all in the tombs will hear his voice, adding a summons from the life-giving judge.

basis: all in tombs hear the judge's voice
note: Jesus says that all who are in tombs will hear his voice. It supplies the universal summons that precedes the two resurrection outcomes in the following verse and the commentary's standing scene.

basis: resurrection of life or judgment
note: The commentary separates the guided from the astray under final judgment; John says those who did good come out to resurrection of life and those who did evil to resurrection of judgment, giving an explicit two-outcome scene.

basis: resurrection of life and resurrection of judgment
note: Those in the tombs come out either to resurrection of life or resurrection of judgment. It gives the commentary's standing resurrection its two-sided outcome.

basis: sins and debtors in prayer
note: The commentary distinguishes the source word dīn from the related deyn debt; Jesus' prayer asks forgiveness of sins while naming those indebted to the speakers, explicitly joining moral fault to debt language.

basis: forgiven sins and forgiven debtors
note: Luke's prayer asks forgiveness of sins because the pray-ers forgive everyone indebted to them. It makes the commentary's proximity of debt and recompense into an explicit moral and devotional analogy.

basis: no release until the last lepton is paid
note: Jesus' legal warning ends with payment of the last small coin before release. It provides the commentary's exact-price and due-debt image in a judicial setting.

basis: steward commanded to render an account
note: The steward must give an account of management before losing his position; the following scene concerns debtors and their bills. It supplies an administrative form of the commentary's account-and-debt imagery.

basis: debtor's bill and amount owed to the master
note: A steward asks a debtor how much is owed to his master and works from the written bill. This gives the debtors and documents that make the preceding command to render an account concrete.

basis: king returns and calls servants to account
note: After receiving kingship, the returning ruler summons servants to learn what their trading has gained. Kingship, commercial calculation, and reckoning meet in one parable.

basis: full, pressed, shaken, overflowing measure returned
note: Jesus promises a good measure, pressed down and shaken together, returned into the giver's lap, and adds that the measure used returns to its user. This turns the commentary's full measure into a precise reciprocity formula.

basis: creditor forgives two debts
note: The commentary distinguishes a due debt from its final repayment; Jesus tells of two debtors unable to repay whom one creditor freely forgives, showing debt as a measure of mercy as well as liability.

basis: the Son of Man's life as ransom
note: The commentary invokes a day when no offered substitute can be accepted; Mark calls the Son of Man's life a ransom for many. The shared payment image leads to a specifically Christian resolution rather than a general commercial analogy.

basis: account on the day of judgment
note: The commentary makes dīn an account and repayment; Jesus says people will give an account for careless words on the day of judgment, extending the reckoning to speech.

basis: account on the day of judgment
note: Jesus says people will render account for every careless word on the day of judgment. The explicit account sharpens the commentary's dīn as reckoning, including what might otherwise be forgotten.

basis: no exchange for one's life
note: The commentary says no equivalent can be offered on that day; Jesus asks what a person could give in exchange for life after gaining the world and losing himself, sharpening the limit on substitution.

basis: exchange for one's life
note: Jesus asks what a person could give in exchange for his life. It is a direct New Testament formulation of the commentary's final limit on offering an equivalent or ransom.

basis: Son of Man comes and repays each person
note: The commentary joins the arriving day, sovereign rule and recompense; Jesus says the Son of Man comes in the Father's glory and repays each according to conduct, a direct Christian formulation of that combined scene.

basis: coming judge repays each according to practice
note: The verse following the question about an exchange for life says the Son of Man will come and repay each according to practice. It keeps ransom's limit and deed-for-deed recompense together.

basis: king settles accounts
note: The commentary joins malik, account and due debt; Jesus' kingdom parable begins with a king settling accounts with his servants, embodying sovereign judgment as creditor.

basis: king settling accounts with servants
note: Jesus likens the kingdom to a king who begins to settle accounts with his servants; the king, reckoning, and unpaid obligation form a direct narrative counterpart to the commentary's ruler of the day of account.

basis: unpayable debt
note: The commentary's debt image reaches a due reckoning; the first servant owes ten thousand talents and cannot pay, making the account's imbalance concrete.

basis: debt released by compassion
note: The commentary presents repayment as the day’s governing image; this king instead feels compassion and cancels the servant’s debt, adding mercy as a complication within a royal account.

basis: debt reinstated; punishment
note: The commentary links unpaid obligation with judgment; after the servant refuses mercy, the king hands him over until the debt is paid, joining debt collection to punishment.

basis: debt exacted under punishment
note: In the same parable the master hands the debtor over until the whole debt is paid. It makes the commentary's due debt and punitive recompense a single judicial action.

basis: the Son of Man sits on a glorious throne
note: The commentary calls the day the sovereign's domain; Jesus' judgment scene opens with the Son of Man coming in glory and sitting on his throne, adding the ruler's enthronement before the separation already described nearby.

basis: royal throne of final judgment
note: The Son of Man comes in glory and sits on his glorious throne. This supplies a visibly royal form for the commentary's owner and ruler of the judgment day.

basis: nations separated before the king
note: The commentary distinguishes the graced from the angered and astray; Jesus gathers all nations before the enthroned Son of Man and separates people as a shepherd separates sheep and goats, making the division a judgment scene.

basis: all nations gathered and separated before the throne
note: All nations are gathered before the enthroned Son of Man and separated as sheep from goats. It supplies the assembled-humanity action between the royal throne and the divergent final rewards.

basis: punishment or life
note: The commentary contrasts those under anger with those guided on the favored path; Jesus' judgment ends in eternal punishment for one group and eternal life for the other, giving the separation its final stakes.

basis: eternal punishment and eternal life
note: The final separation ends in eternal punishment for one group and eternal life for the other. It states the opposed outcomes implied by the commentary's recompense and divine wrath.

basis: settle with an accuser before court
note: The commentary makes a debt due under judgment its central image; Jesus tells a debtor to settle with his accuser on the way to court before the judge hands him over, adding urgency before a judicial account closes.

basis: last coin owed until paid
note: The commentary links a full-weight coin to the debt's final settlement; Jesus says the prisoner will not leave until paying the last quadrans, making even a small coin part of complete collection.

basis: forgive debts as debtors are forgiven
note: Matthew's prayer names moral forgiveness as the mutual release of debts. It gives a New Testament path by which commercial obligation is transposed into accountability before God.

basis: two gates and opposed ways
note: The commentary asks for the straight path and marks out the astray; Jesus contrasts a wide gate and broad way leading to destruction with the narrow way, making moral direction a choice of route and destination.

basis: constricted way leading to life
note: Jesus contrasts the constricted way leading to life with the broad way to destruction. It gives the commentary's straight path and loss a specific New Testament path-outcome contrast.

basis: measure used becomes measure received
note: Jesus says the measure one uses will be measured back. It turns the commentary's exact measure into a reciprocal ethical rule, though it does not portray a literal final balance.

basis: another person's debt charged to Paul
note: Paul tells Philemon to charge any wrong or debt owed by Onesimus to Paul. This concrete assumption of another's obligation illuminates the commentary's language of putting one thing in another's place.

basis: the world's kingdom becomes the Lord's kingdom
note: At the seventh trumpet the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of God and his Christ, who reigns forever. This gives the commentary's exclusive final sovereignty an apocalyptic Christian formulation.

basis: time for wrath, judgment, and reward
note: The verse announces God's wrath, the time to judge the dead, reward servants, and destroy destroyers. It gives a compact New Testament counterpart to punishment and payment on the decisive day.

basis: blood given to blood-shedders as their due
note: Because the persecutors poured out the blood of saints and prophets, the bowl judgment gives them blood to drink, “for they deserve it.” This makes bloodshed itself the measure of eschatological recompense.

basis: repay, double, and measure back in the cup
note: The heavenly command says to repay Babylon as she repaid, double her works, and mix double in her own cup. It gives the commentary's equivalent return and unbending measure an apocalyptic form.

basis: dead stand; books opened
note: The commentary's resurrection scene has creatures standing before the Sustainer; Revelation shows dead, great and small, standing before the throne as books open and they are judged by their works.

basis: dead stand before throne; books and deeds judged
note: The dead, great and small, stand before the throne; books are opened and they are judged by their deeds. This closely matches the commentary's standing, accounting, and exact recompense scene.

basis: sea and death surrender their dead
note: The commentary says people cannot be absent from the day of account; Revelation says the sea, Death and Hades give up their dead for judgment, closing imagined routes of disappearance.

basis: sea, Death, and Hades return their dead
note: The sea, Death, and Hades give up their dead, after which each is judged by deeds. It provides the return-from-every-custodian detail missing from the commentary's compressed resurrection image.

basis: reward and repayment according to work
note: The returning Lord brings recompense to repay each according to work. It is a concise final-payment counterpart to the commentary's balance and day of return.

basis: martyrs ask when their blood will be avenged
note: The slain cry to the sovereign Judge for judgment and vengeance of their blood on earth. Revelation preserves the commentary's unresolved-blood image inside an explicitly eschatological court appeal.

basis: day of wrath; who can stand?
note: The commentary glosses divine anger as punishment and links q-w-m to standing; Revelation's terrified rulers ask who can stand on the great day of wrath, joining both details in one scene.

basis: great day of wrath and ability to stand
note: Revelation announces the great day of divine wrath and asks who can stand. It directly joins the commentary's two images of punitive anger and rising before the final authority.

basis: black horse carrying a balance
note: Revelation's apocalyptic balance belongs to famine rationing and prices, not an impartial courtroom scale. That different use helps delimit the commentary's moralized, upright-balance image while retaining its economic force.

basis: denarius pricing of grain under the balance
note: The apocalyptic voice fixes grain at a denarius price while preserving oil and wine. It supplies the price-and-coin detail that explains the economic force of the balance in the preceding verse.

basis: exchange truth for a lie
note: The commentary describes hidaya and dalala as a failed trade; Paul says people exchanged God's truth for a lie and worshiped the creature, applying exchange language to misdirected worship.

basis: vengeance belongs to God who repays
note: Paul prohibits private vengeance because God says, “I will repay.” This gives the commentary's account of divine wrath as punitive recompense a disciplined ethical implication.

basis: everyone before God's tribunal
note: The commentary has creation stand before the one who sustains all; Paul says all will stand before God's judgment seat, making universal accountability explicit.

basis: all stand before God's judgment seat
note: Paul says all people will stand before the judgment seat of God. This provides the exact bodily-postural form of the commentary's creatures standing before the living, sustaining Judge.

basis: each gives account to God
note: The commentary frames judgment as an individual account; Paul says each person will give an account of himself to God, making responsibility personal rather than transferable.

basis: each person gives an account to God
note: After saying all stand before God's judgment seat, Paul says each will give an account of self to God. This supplies the verbal accounting element distinct from the physical standing of verse 10.

basis: day of wrath and righteous judgment
note: The commentary treats the day as a certain reckoning and Allah's anger as punishment; Paul names a day of wrath when God's righteous judgment is revealed, supplying a close Christian formulation.

basis: day of wrath and righteous judgment
note: Paul speaks of storing up wrath for the day when God's righteous judgment is revealed. It directly supports the commentary's reading of divine wrath as judicial punishment rather than emotion alone.

basis: repay each according to deeds
note: The commentary glosses din as account and recompense; Paul says God will repay each according to works, giving the day’s balance a direct ethical rule.

basis: God repays each according to works
note: The next verse defines that righteous judgment as repayment according to works. It supplies the commentary's payment-and-balance logic without needing a literal marketplace.

basis: saved from wrath through blood
note: The commentary glosses divine anger as punishment and says no counter-value is accepted that day; Paul says people justified by Christ's blood will be saved from wrath, a distinct Christian account of how judgment is escaped.

basis: Head of Days, throne, books, standing court
note: 1 Enoch depicts the Head of Days seated on the throne of glory, books opened, and the heavenly court standing. It is an unusually close Second Temple expansion of the commentary's ruler, standing, and account scene.

basis: the earth and Sheol return their deposits
note: At the resurrection the earth and Sheol give back what was entrusted to them. The return of what is owed gives the commentary's due-payment image a resurrection form.

basis: kings stand before the enthroned one
note: The commentary places humanity standing before the life-sustainer on the day of account; 1 Enoch says kings and mighty ones stand before the enthroned Elect One, extending the reckoning to earthly rulers.

basis: kings see the enthroned judge and righteous judgment
note: The kings, mighty, and landowners see the glorious enthroned figure and recognize that righteous judgment proceeds before him. It gives the commentary's ruler-and-day scene a Second Temple reversal of earthly power.

basis: lots of light and darkness
note: The commentary names a straight way, those favored, and those astray; the Community Rule describes humanity divided between spirits and ways of light and darkness until visitation, adding a Second Temple Jewish account of opposed paths and outcomes.

basis: hope of resurrection after death
note: The commentary links q-w-m with the resurrection before the Sustainer; the tortured martyr says the King of the world will raise those who die for his laws, adding a Jewish resurrection hope grounded in fidelity.

basis: the dead restored from dust
note: The commentary connects the straight-path root label to resurrection and standing; 4 Ezra says earth and dust will restore those sleeping in them, adding a detailed restoration scene before judgment.

basis: earth and dust give up the dead
note: 4 Ezra says earth and dust surrender those asleep in them, and the storehouses surrender souls. It supplies a detailed Jewish apocalyptic counterpart to the commentary's resurrection day.

basis: Most High revealed at judgment seat
note: The commentary presents the day as the sovereign's account; 4 Ezra says the Most High is revealed at the judgment seat, while compassion and patience withdraw, giving the scene an explicitly judicial climax.

basis: the Most High appears on the judgment seat
note: Immediately after the dead are returned, 4 Ezra places the Most High on the judgment seat. The sequence aligns resurrection with the sovereign's final adjudication.

basis: deeds follow and reward is displayed
note: 4 Ezra says the work follows the person and the reward is displayed. It fills out the prior judgment-seat scene with the commentary's exact return for what was done.

basis: din ve-heshbon before the King of kings
note: The commentary calls the day a judgment and account under its Mālik; Avot says each person will give din ve-heshbon, “judgment and account,” before the King of kings, using the Hebrew cognate in the same paired sense.

basis: shop, credit, open ledger, collectors
note: Avot turns deferred credit into a moral accounting image: the shop gives credit, the ledger records it, and collectors exact payment. This closely supplies the commentary's debt, due date, record, and final recompense picture.

basis: Hillel's prosbul and sabbatical debts
note: Hillel's prosbul responds to lenders withholding loans as the release year approaches, reworking Deuteronomy's debt law through a court procedure. It shows a rabbinic legal reading of how written obligation and mercy coexist.

basis: seven chronological questions for witnesses
note: The Mishnah tests witnesses by sabbatical cycle, year, month, day, hour, and place. It offers a later Jewish legal answer to the commentary's concern that a witness may lose the event from memory.

basis: by the measure one measures, so one is measured
note: The Mishnah states its measure-for-measure principle while interpreting the sotah ordeal. It gives later Jewish formulation to the commentary's balance as equivalent retribution rather than mere market accuracy.

basis: lend in need and repay on time
note: Sirach instructs one to lend to a neighbor in need and repay the neighbor at the appointed time. It closely parallels the commentary's concrete debt with a fixed term before that debt becomes an image of judgment.

basis: Abel's blood expanded to future righteous descendants
note: This Palestinian Targum expands Abel's crying blood to include the blood of righteous descendants yet to arise. It intensifies the commentary's claim that blood does not disappear, though wording varies among Targum witnesses.

basis: deeds weighed at judgment
note: The commentary develops the exact balance and full-weight coin as an image of judgment; the Testament depicts deeds weighed for a soul, adding a Jewish apocalyptic scene in which moral outcome is literally assessed on scales.

basis: postmortem tribunal, records, and Dokiel's balance
note: In Recension A, souls pass a postmortem tribunal in which deeds are recorded and the archangel Dokiel weighs them. The vision gathers the commentary's standing, accounting, and scale images; chapter divisions vary by edition.

basis: deeds weighed by YHWH
note: Hannah calls YHWH a God of knowledge by whom deeds are weighed. This condenses the commentary's claim that conduct is assessed by a precise, nonpartial standard.

basis: day of YHWH as darkness, not light
note: Those who desire YHWH's day are warned that it is darkness rather than light. This gives the commentary's severe event-day a prophetic reversal of complacent expectation.

basis: false measures and scales
note: The commentary brings fraudulent weighing beside the day people stand; Amos depicts merchants shrinking the measure and enlarging the shekel, giving the crooked scale a concrete injustice against the poor.

basis: false balances in grain trade
note: Amos exposes merchants who shrink the measure, enlarge the shekel, and falsify balances. It gives the commentary's cheated measure a prophetic social setting in which such trade is itself judged.

basis: God will not forget injustice
note: The commentary notes the witness whose memory may fail and the blood that can be lost unavenged; after exposing false measures Amos swears God will never forget their deeds, making divine memory answer human evasion.

basis: stand in allotted place at the end of days
note: Daniel is told to rest and then stand in his allotted place at the end of days. This is an unusually direct pairing of resurrection-like standing and the final temporal horizon developed in the commentary.

basis: sleepers awake to opposed outcomes
note: The commentary connects q-w-m with resurrection before the Sustainer; Daniel says sleepers in the dust awake, some to everlasting life and some to disgrace, supplying both the rising and the divided result.

basis: awakening from dust to life or disgrace
note: Daniel's sleepers in the dust awake, some to everlasting life and some to abhorrence. It gives the commentary's standing resurrection a divided recompense.

basis: weighed and found deficient
note: The commentary's full-weight coin and unyielding balance meet Daniel's verdict on Belshazzar: he is weighed and found deficient as his kingdom ends, making the scale a ruler's judgment.

basis: a king weighed in balances
note: Daniel tells Belshazzar that he has been weighed in the balances and found deficient. The judgment of a ruler through a balance directly realizes the commentary's kingly day and exact scale.

basis: court sits; books open
note: The commentary makes yawm al-din a day of reckoning under the sovereign; Daniel's Aramaic court sits and books open for judgment, adding an apocalyptic courtroom with deeds recorded.

basis: Aramaic דִּינָא, judgment
note: The source commentary explicitly labels ٱلدِّينِ and glosses it as ḥisāb and recompense; Daniel's Aramaic דִּינָא names the court/judgment as it sits. This is a judicial cognate, while the commentary still distinguishes Arabic dīn from deyn debt.

basis: Aramaic dînâ, court, opened books
note: The commentary's dīn as judgment and account meets Daniel's Aramaic dînâ: the court sits and books are opened, giving the cognate root a concrete eschatological reckoning scene.

basis: dominion given to the humanlike figure
note: The commentary makes the day God's sovereign domain; after the court scene, Daniel gives the humanlike figure everlasting dominion and a kingdom, adding a royal succession scene within judgment.

basis: Aramaic malku, everlasting kingdom
note: The commentary's m-l-k identifies the day’s sovereign; Daniel's Aramaic malku, “kingdom,” shares that Semitic root and names an everlasting dominion granted in the court vision.

basis: the court removes the ruler's dominion
note: The commentary defines the malik branch through authority and command; Daniel's court sits to remove the persecuting ruler's dominion, showing judgment as an actual transfer of power.

basis: court sits and a ruler's dominion is removed
note: Daniel's court sits and strips the hostile ruler of dominion for destruction. It supplies a concrete court-scene counterpart to the commentary's claim that human possession and command fail on the day of judgment.

basis: Ancient of Days seated on a throne
note: Daniel's Ancient of Days takes his flaming throne before the court convenes. It supplies a royal judicial scene for the commentary's owner of the decisive day.

basis: seventh-year debt release
note: The commentary brings a deferred debt into the judgment image; Deuteronomy announces remission at the end of every seven years, supplying the legal timing and social practice behind a debt's due term.

basis: release of debts in the seventh year
note: The commentary uses a loan due at its term to illuminate the final account; Deuteronomy commands creditors to release claims at the sabbatical year, adding a Torah practice of debt remission rather than final collection.

basis: sabbatical release of a loan
note: The sabbatical law requires a creditor to release what was lent to a neighbor. It offers a Torah counterpoint to the commentary's debt coming due: a fixed time can cancel rather than exact an obligation.

basis: Hebrew yaqum; witnesses establish a matter
note: The commentary joins q-w-m, standing, and a witness who may forget. Deuteronomy's yaqum, from Hebrew qûm, says one witness cannot “rise” alone and requires corroborating testimony to establish a matter.

basis: life for life; no pity
note: The commentary's qisas branch describes a life claim that can be converted to blood-price; Deuteronomy states life for life and forbids pity, supplying the retributive baseline that makes the conversion a meaningful difference.

basis: full weight and measure
note: The commentary's “standing” coin has exact weight and does not tip the scale; Deuteronomy requires a full and just weight, making commercial accuracy a covenant obligation.

basis: whole and just weight
note: The command for a whole and just weight and measure gives a legal analogue to the commentary's full-weight coin that does not tip the scale.

basis: vengeance and recompense reserved for a day
note: The commentary glosses dīn as recompense and makes the day an arriving event; Moses' song says vengeance and recompense are reserved for the day when the enemy's foot slips, joining both images in one judgment formula.

basis: vengeance, recompense, and a coming day
note: “To me belong vengeance and recompense” is followed by the nearness of calamity. It closely joins the commentary's divine punitive anger, payment in return, and inevitable day.

basis: Hebrew יָדִין, “he will judge”
note: The source commentary labels ٱلدِّينِ and explicitly glosses it as judgment/account; Moses' song uses the Hebrew d-y-n cognate when YHWH judges his people, supporting the judicial sense without equating the Arabic word's full range.

basis: every deed brought to judgment
note: The commentary treats the day as a comprehensive account; Ecclesiastes says God brings every deed, including what is hidden, into judgment, spelling out why no action escapes the reckoning.

basis: God brings every hidden deed into judgment
note: Ecclesiastes says God brings every deed, including hidden good or evil, into judgment. It supplies the commentary's claim that no person can be absent from or concealed in the account.

basis: ransom for an ox owner's liability
note: The commentary says a life claim can be converted to blood-price and later says no ransom works on the judgment day; Exodus permits a ransom for the owner of a lethal ox, a sharply bounded Torah case that clarifies which kind of liability can be exchanged for payment.

basis: ransom imposed for a life
note: Where an owner is liable after his ox kills, Exodus allows a ransom imposed for his life. Read beside Numbers 35 and the commentary, it shows that biblical law distinguishes cases in which a life-payment can and cannot replace liability.

basis: righteous people cannot deliver another's life
note: The commentary says no one can replace another's liability on the day; Ezekiel says even Noah, Daniel and Job would deliver only themselves, not sons or daughters, specifying the limit on a righteous person's rescue of kin.

basis: one bears one's own iniquity
note: The commentary's final account admits no substitute payment; Ezekiel says the son does not bear the father's guilt and the sinner's own soul dies, making responsibility individual.

basis: just balances, ephah, and bath
note: Ezekiel's restored commonwealth is ordered to use just balances and standard measures. It gives the commentary's upright scale a public, ruler-governed economic setting.

basis: silver and gold cannot satisfy or deliver in wrath
note: Ezekiel has people cast away silver and gold because it cannot deliver them on the day of YHWH's wrath. The image explicitly turns valuable payment into useless weight at judgment.

basis: Abel's blood cries to God
note: The commentary's branch gloss says blood can go to waste if vengeance is not taken; God tells Cain Abel's blood cries from the ground, a contrary image in which murdered blood remains heard even before human vengeance.

basis: Abel's blood cries from the ground
note: The commentary fears blood going lost when it is not avenged; Abel's blood cries from the ground to God, making shed blood an enduring claimant rather than a forgotten event.

basis: God demands an account for blood
note: The commentary's branch gloss says blood may be lost if not avenged; Genesis says God will require an accounting for human blood, adding explicit divine reckoning for bloodshed.

basis: day of YHWH, wrath, sinners destroyed
note: Isaiah calls the coming day cruel, full of wrath and fierce anger, to destroy sinners. It supplies another prophetic rendering of the commentary's day as a devastating event rather than a neutral unit of time.

basis: dead live and corpses rise
note: Isaiah summons the dead to live and the corpses to rise. This is a direct resurrection counterpart to the commentary's qiyāmah, when creatures stand before God.

basis: Hebrew yequmun, “they shall rise”
note: The commentary develops q-w-m from upright standing to resurrection; Isaiah's yequmun, “they shall rise,” uses the Hebrew cognate qûm in an actual resurrection proclamation, not merely a lexical resemblance.

basis: the earth reveals blood and no longer covers its slain
note: In Isaiah's judgment setting, the earth discloses its bloodshed and stops concealing those killed. It joins the commentary's resurrection setting to its image of blood that cannot vanish without answer.

basis: the righteous path made level
note: The commentary asks for the straight path and connects it to a balance that will not lean; Isaiah says the righteous one's path is level, adding a biblical image of moral direction made even.

basis: level path of the righteous made level by the Upright One
note: Isaiah calls the righteous person's path level and addresses God as the Upright One who makes it level. It complements the commentary's straight-path image, though it does not itself use a scale.

basis: Hebrew מלכנו, “our king”
note: The source labels مَٰلِكِ with root م ل ك and describes its royal command; Isaiah calls YHWH judge, lawgiver and “our king” in one verse, showing the cognate royal term in a judicial setting.

basis: YHWH as judge, lawgiver, and king
note: Isaiah names YHWH judge, lawgiver, and king in one confession. It makes concrete the commentary's definition of the sovereign as one who rules by command and prohibition.

basis: day of vengeance and year of recompense
note: Isaiah names a day of YHWH's vengeance and a year of recompense. It explicitly pairs a decisive time with retaliation and payment.

basis: a holy way where the unclean do not pass or go astray
note: Isaiah's eschatological highway is called the holy way; the unclean do not pass on it and even fools do not go astray. It is a close path-and-non-straying counterpart to the commentary's straight path and its contrary ending.

basis: coming ruler brings recompense
note: The commentary's king has a strong hand and the day arrives with repayment; Isaiah says the Lord comes with might, his arm rules, and recompense is with him, meeting sovereignty and repayment in one image.

basis: Egypt given as Israel's ransom and exchange
note: Isaiah pictures God giving Egypt, Cush, and Seba as Israel's ransom or exchange. Its historical divine substitution contrasts with the commentary's final-day claim that an offered equivalent cannot be accepted.

basis: YHWH enters judgment with all flesh
note: Isaiah says YHWH enters into judgment with all flesh by fire and sword. It directly combines the commentary's universal judgment, wrath, and punitive outcome.

basis: exchange glory for what is worthless
note: The commentary's source gloss makes guidance and misguidance opposite sides of a failed purchase; Jeremiah says Israel exchanged its glory for what does not profit, giving the bad exchange a covenantal setting.

basis: sealed deed, witnesses, weighed silver
note: Jeremiah's land purchase is written and sealed, witnessed, and paid by weighing silver on scales. Its own legal transaction joins the commentary's written obligation, witnesses, price, and even balance imagery.

basis: deeds preserved for many days
note: Jeremiah orders the sealed and open deeds stored so they may last many days. It adds durable documentary memory to the commentary's concern that a witness can forget an obligation.

basis: weighed in just balance
note: The commentary hears “straight” in the perfectly balanced coin; Job asks to be weighed in a just balance so God may know his integrity, making straight measure a moral test.

basis: weighed in a just balance before God
note: Job asks to be weighed in a just balance so that God may know his integrity. The balance is already a personal divine verdict, not only a rule for merchants.

basis: “a ransom has been found” for one going to the pit
note: Job's heavenly mediator says a ransom has been found and the sufferer should be spared descent to the pit. Its rescue-payment image contrasts with the commentary's final-day refusal of ransom and marks the contextual limit of that refusal.

basis: God repays each according to work
note: Job's speaker says God repays humans according to their work and lets each find what accords with their way. It gives the commentary's equivalent payment a direct wisdom formulation.

basis: great and very terrible day
note: Joel calls the day of YHWH great and exceedingly terrible and asks who can endure it. Its question of endurance complements the commentary's scene of people standing before the Judge.

basis: just weights and balances
note: The commentary makes the upright path a balance that does not lean; Leviticus commands honest scales, stones and measures, grounding the image in Israel's market law.

basis: just scales, weights, ephah, and hin
note: Leviticus requires just scales and measures in Israel's market. It supplies the ordinary ethical practice behind the commentary's image of an upright balance in the final account.

basis: who can stand on the day of his coming
note: Malachi asks who can endure and stand when the Lord appears. The verse binds the commentary's day, standing before the living Judge, and purgative punishment in one scene.

basis: judgment on wage fraud and perjury
note: The commentary joins divine judgment with crooked weighing and a witness who might fail; Malachi says God comes near to judge those who oppress wage-earners and swear falsely, making economic and testimonial injustice explicit charges.

basis: nations taught to walk in God's paths
note: The commentary asks for guidance on the straight path; Micah pictures nations going to Zion to be taught God's ways and walk in his paths, adding a public, communal destination to the prayer for guidance.

basis: God judges and arbitrates among nations
note: The commentary places the path under the sovereign's judgment; Micah says God judges among peoples and arbitrates for many nations, connecting divine rule to just decisions among communities.

basis: acquittal and wicked balances
note: The commentary joins fraudulent weighing to final accounting; Micah asks whether one can acquit someone who uses wicked scales and deceitful weights, making the crooked balance a matter for judgment.

basis: acquittal and fraudulent scales
note: Micah asks whether God can acquit someone with wicked scales and false weights. It explicitly fuses courtroom acquittal with commercial fraud, as the commentary fuses judgment day and a tilted balance.

basis: no ransom for a murderer
note: The commentary's root branch describes a death claim changed into blood-price; Torah law forbids taking ransom for a murderer, a concrete legal difference about whether payment can replace the life-for-life claim.

basis: no ransom for a murderer
note: The commentary notes retaliation may be turned to blood-money when the victim's kin forgive; Numbers forbids taking a ransom for a murderer liable to death. The contrast marks a concrete legal difference about substitution for bloodshed.

basis: no payment to return from refuge
note: The commentary develops substitute payment and blood-price as possible exchanges; Numbers also bars a ransom for a killer to return from refuge before the high priest's death, specifying a second boundary on monetary substitution.

basis: blood pollution; only the killer's blood atones
note: The commentary's root branch describes a death claim converted to blood-price; Numbers says blood pollutes the land and homicide cannot be atoned for except by the blood of the one who shed it, a specific legal contrast to monetary substitution.

basis: unatoned blood and the land
note: Numbers says bloodshed pollutes the land and is not expiated except by the shedder's blood. It gives a legal-theological form to the commentary's fear that spilled blood must not simply disappear without answer.

basis: false balance versus a full weight
note: A false balance is an abomination while a full weight delights YHWH. The proverb directly supplies the commentary's contrast between a tipped scale and its exact, acceptable counterweight.

basis: riches do not profit on the day of wrath
note: The proverb denies that riches profit on the day of wrath, while righteousness delivers from death. It sharply qualifies the commentary's debt-and-value imagery at the final account.

basis: balances belong to the Lord
note: The commentary imagines the final measure as a perfectly straight scale; Proverbs says honest balances and weights belong to the Lord, linking fairness in commerce to divine authority.

basis: just balance and weights belong to YHWH
note: The commentary places a true balance within God's final reckoning; this proverb says the just balance, scales, and bag-weights are YHWH's work, grounding the image in divine rather than merely commercial justice.

basis: borrower servant to lender
note: The proverb says the borrower becomes servant to the lender. It gives the commentary's loan relation a concrete hierarchy of power that complicates its image of sovereign ownership.

basis: buy truth; do not sell it
note: The commentary depicts guidance and error as the two sides of a bad trade; Proverbs says to buy truth and not sell it, treating moral knowledge as something whose value must be guarded.

basis: God weighs hearts and repays
note: The commentary says no one disappears from the day's account; Proverbs says the one who weighs hearts knows and repays each according to his work, joining hidden knowledge with recompense.

basis: God weighs hearts and repays deeds
note: The proverb says the one who weighs hearts knows and repays each person according to work. It makes the commentary's unleaning balance explicitly a divine assessment followed by measured payment.

basis: standing in judgment; two groups
note: The commentary links the q-w-m root label on “straight” to people rising before God; Psalm 1 says the wicked will not stand in judgment or among the righteous, joining judgment posture to the division of ways.

basis: Hebrew יָקֻמוּ, “stand”
note: The source labels ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ with root ق و م and explicitly connects that family to rising; Psalm 1 uses Hebrew יָקֻמוּ for the wicked not standing in judgment, a cognate standing sense rather than a claim that both words mean “straight.”

basis: wicked do not stand in judgment
note: The psalm says the wicked will not stand in the judgment, supplying a precise biblical reverse of the commentary's picture of creatures standing before the Sustainer on the resurrection day.

basis: wicked borrows and does not repay
note: The psalm contrasts the wicked borrower who does not repay with the righteous giver. It supplies the commentary's ordinary debt-and-payment image in a moral distinction, though not a final court scene.

basis: God alone redeems from Sheol
note: After saying no person can ransom a brother, the psalmist says God will redeem his life from Sheol; this qualifies the commentary's no-exchange image by locating rescue with God rather than a human payer.

basis: no human ransom for a life
note: The commentary says no offered equivalent is accepted on that day; the psalm says no person can redeem a brother or give God a ransom for his life, closely specifying the limit of human substitution.

basis: no human ransom can be given to God
note: The commentary says no substitute payment is accepted on the final day; this psalm denies that a person can give God a ransom for a brother, making the limit of monetary exchange explicit.

basis: the price of life's redemption is beyond reach
note: The commentary develops price, equivalent and full measure, then says a ransom cannot settle the final account; the psalm says life's redemption is too costly and beyond payment, explaining why no human can buy another free.

basis: repayment according to deeds
note: The commentary explains dīn as recompense and equal payment; the psalm says the Lord repays each person according to his deed, matching that account-and-return sense.

basis: God remembers blood and the afflicted cry
note: The commentary speaks of blood lost if it is not avenged; the psalm says the seeker of blood remembers and does not forget the afflicted. Divine remembrance answers the image of vanished blood.

basis: YHWH comes to judge the earth
note: The commentary describes the day as an event that arrives and the balance as just measure; the psalm says YHWH comes to judge the world in righteousness, making arrival and equitable judgment one scene.

basis: YHWH comes to judge earth in righteousness
note: The psalm announces YHWH's coming to judge the world in righteousness and peoples in faithfulness. Its universal, equitable judgment fills out the commentary's claim that the day is a true accounting.

basis: YHWH king over all earth “on that day”
note: The commentary's day transfers undivided rule to its Mālik; Zechariah says YHWH will be king over all the earth and, on that day, one with one name. It makes royal exclusivity explicitly eschatological.

basis: the approaching day of the Lord
note: The commentary presents yawm as a severe event that arrives; Zephaniah calls the great day of the Lord near and hastening, adding a prophetic day-of-judgment formula.

basis: Hebrew יום יהוה, “day of the Lord”
note: The source commentary labels يَوْمِ and develops it as an arriving judgment event; Zephaniah uses the cognate Hebrew יוֹם in its approaching “day of the Lord,” placing the judgment in a shared Semitic day formula.

basis: day of wrath and distress
note: The commentary reads divine anger as punitive retribution; Zephaniah describes the day as wrath, distress and ruin, specifying the judgment's felt consequence.

basis: day of wrath, distress, ruin, darkness
note: Zephaniah layers several “days” within the day of YHWH: wrath, distress, devastation, darkness. It is a close biblical realization of the commentary's severe day that bears many events within it.

basis: silver and gold cannot deliver on the day of wrath
note: Zephaniah says neither silver nor gold can deliver on YHWH's day of wrath. It is a direct biblical counterpart to the commentary's claim that a final substitute payment is not accepted.

basis: the righteous stand before their oppressors
note: The commentary connects rising to the final division of people; Wisdom says the righteous will stand with confidence before those who afflicted them, adding a reversal in which the formerly oppressed are vindicated.

basis: erring from the way of truth
note: The commentary distinguishes the favored path from those who stray; the wicked in Wisdom's postmortem confession say they wandered from the way of truth, adding a scene where the astray recognize their error after the righteous are vindicated.

basis: weary paths of lawlessness
note: The commentary contrasts a straight path with misguidance; the same confession says the wicked wearied themselves on paths of lawlessness, making the failed route a life of chosen conduct.

basis: rulers examined by God
note: The commentary defines the malik branch as one with command and authority; Wisdom says rulers received sovereignty from God, who will examine their works, making earthly rule answerable to the final sovereign.

basis: unjust rulers are judged for not walking rightly
note: The commentary defines the malik branch as command over a community and connects the straight path to right conduct; Wisdom rebukes rulers for not ruling rightly or walking according to God's will, tying royal authority to a path by which it is judged.

basis: severe judgment for rulers
note: Wisdom warns that a severe judgment comes upon those in high places. It turns the commentary's kingly hierarchy back upon human rulers, who too face the sovereign Judge.

basis: one deed tips the balance
note: The commentary's straight path is also a balance that does not tilt; Kiddushin says a person should view the world as evenly balanced and one commandment can tip it toward merit, turning ethical choice into a decisive measure.

basis: books opened on New Year
note: The commentary describes a day when deeds are accounted and outcomes differ; the Talmud says books are opened on Rosh Hashanah and distinguishes righteous, wicked and intermediate people, adding a Jewish liturgical calendar for judgment.

basis: all pass before God; three books opened
note: The rabbinic account of Rosh Hashanah has all creatures pass before God and speaks of heavenly books for verdicts. It interprets judgment and record imagery as an annually enacted reckoning.

basis: first judgment question concerns honest business
note: The commentary develops debt, exchange and dishonest scales as ethical matters; the Talmud says a person is first asked at judgment whether business was conducted faithfully, bringing commercial honesty directly into the afterlife account.

basis: “Did you conduct business faithfully?”
note: At heavenly judgment, faithful business dealing is named among the first questions asked. It directly carries the commentary's market-scale ethics into personal eschatological accountability.

basis: credit, ledger, collectors
note: The commentary makes the appointed day the settlement of debt; Avot pictures the world as a shop with credit, an open ledger, and collectors exacting payment, an unusually close Jewish accounting image.

basis: dead revived; living judged
note: The commentary links the q-w-m branch to resurrection and people standing before God; Avot says the dead will live again and the living will be judged, an especially compact Jewish formulation of the whole scene.

basis: no forgetfulness, favoritism or bribes
note: The commentary notes witness-memory failure and says an offered equivalent is rejected; Avot says the Judge has no forgetting, favoritism or acceptance of bribes and that all is according to reckoning, directly sharpening both details.
